findings.description: SHEET-FORMULA-002 says the system shall write EACH per-row formula 'as references to that row's own cells.' The real code's row-anchored formulas split into two structurally different classes: (1) Market Value `=E{r}*B{r}`, Unrealized P&L `=F{r}-D{r}`, Est. Unrealized Tax `=G{r}*H{r}`, Net Unrealized `=G{r}*(1-H{r})`, Unrealized % `=IF(D{r}=0,0,G{r}/D{r})` — these DO reference that row's own cells, matching the spec text; but (2) Price `=GOOGLEFINANCE("{ticker}","price")` and Quote Date `=IFERROR(TEXT(INT(GOOGLEFINANCE("{ticker}","tradetime"))-DATE(1970,1,1),"0"),"")` — the two formulas built around the crate's headline live-price oracle — contain ZERO cell references of any kind. The ticker is resolved via `AliasMap::resolve` in Rust and baked into the formula text as a quoted literal; there is no `=GOOGLEFINANCE(A{r},"price")`-style cell reference to a Symbol/ticker column. Row-shift safety for these two columns is achieved by an entirely different mechanism the spec text doesn't name: the whole tab is rewritten wholesale (tail-truncate + full replace) every publish, so the literal ticker is regenerated in lockstep with whatever row it lands on, rather than being protected by a same-row cell reference. All three A-direction sketches, working from the spec text alone, unanimously modeled 'per-row formula' as universally row/cell-parameterized (RowFormulaFn/RowFormulaSpec/template all take `row` as the sole substitution axis) and used a cell-referencing GOOGLEFINANCE example (e.g. A1's `GOOGLEFINANCE(B{row},...)`) — none anticipated a formula class with zero cell references. All three B-direction reconstructions, working from the code alone, independently and explicitly separated the 5 cell-referencing arithmetic formulas from the 2 ticker-literal GOOGLEFINANCE formulas (B2 and B3 state this split as two distinct EARS clauses; B1 gives the same formula texts though states the 'reference only that row's own cells' rule more generally without flagging the tension). Both directions converge on the same real gap: the spec's blanket 'each per-row formula' language does not hold for the crate's own live-price oracle formulas.

The real test `per_row_formulas_reference_their_own_row_beneath_frozen_header` (formula.rs) — the test that most directly operationalizes SHEET-FORMULA-002's 'so a row shift cannot mis-pair them' clause — asserts the no-other-row-leaked check, across every row, ONLY for Market Value and Unrealized P&L. Est. Unrealized Tax, Net Unrealized, and Unrealized % are checked for correct same-row references in a different test (`positions_shows_pretax_and_live_posttax_estimate`), and only at the single first row (`r = DATA_START_ROW`), never checked for absence of other-row leakage across multiple rows. The GOOGLEFINANCE Price/Quote-Date formulas are structurally exempt from any row-leak assertion (they contain no row numbers to leak). So the code's own test suite pins a narrower, column-specific version of the row-shift-safety guarantee than SHEET-FORMULA-002's uniform wording implies — visible by comparing what B1/B2/B3 (working only from the tests) could actually cite in support of 'no cross-row leakage' versus the blanket spec claim.

runtime/adapters.rs defines the History tab's anchored data range via an independently hardcoded literal, `const HISTORY_DATA_RANGE_SUFFIX: &str = "!A2:Z";`, rather than referencing `sheets_view::DATA_START_ROW` the way `ViewSheetsAdapter::data_range` does (`format!("'{name}'!A{}:Z", sheets_view::DATA_START_ROW)`). The two numerically agree today (both anchor at row 2), but 'a fixed anchored start row' is actually two separately-maintained literals in the codebase, not the single named constant the spec's phrasing (and all three A sketches, which modeled `DATA_START_ROW` as one shared constant) assumed. Lower-confidence / likely out of SHEET-FORMULA-002's direct scope since History is owned by `reports`, not `sheets-view`, and the requirement's 'sheets-view' framing centers on the Positions-style live-formula tabs — noted as a minor tangential observation, not the primary finding.

notes:
Core constants/mechanisms are coherent across both directions and the real code: DATA_START_ROW = 2 as a compile-time constant (header row 1, data from row 2), full wholesale rewrite of the data range on every republish (never incremental diff), and the frozen header's byte-identical never-rewritten invariant (enforced by an `assert_eq!` in testkit's InMemorySheetsView) are all correctly predicted by every A run and correctly reconstructed by every B run — no drift there.

The one substantive, high-confidence finding (finding 1) is genuinely bidirectional: it is traceable to explicit spec text on the A side (the spec's 'each per-row formula...references to that row's own cells' forced all three A sketches into a uniform row/cell-substitution design that the real GOOGLEFINANCE columns don't follow) and is independently, concretely visible on the B side (all three B reconstructions reproduce the exact ticker-literal formula text and — B2/B3 more explicitly than B1 — separate it from the cell-referencing arithmetic formulas). That convergence is why I called this BD-DRIFT rather than B-ONLY-DRIFT despite the B-side detail being richer.

Minor A-run divergence (not counted as a finding): A1 leaves column-letter identity as an opaque caller-supplied string (implicitly supports AA+), A2 explicitly implements full base-26 A1 column-letter arithmetic, A3 explicitly restricts to single-letter A-Z columns and flags the restriction. The real code (`fn cell_ref(col: char, row: u32)`) only ever needs single-letter columns (max 13 columns, A-M) so this variance among A runs doesn't surface as an actual code-vs-spec drift, just differing generality choices — mentioned for completeness, not listed as a finding.

Findings 2 and 3 are B-only and secondary: finding 2 is a test-coverage precision gap rather than an enforced-but-undocumented behavior; finding 3 is tangential (likely belongs to a different owning segment/EARS ID, `reports`'s History tab, not `sheets-view`'s Positions formulas) and is flagged at lower confidence.
